::: {.bridge}
Six sessions built one chain: measurable properties, an equation of state, residual properties, fugacity, mixtures, activity. Today we ask of every result: **which model, and what evidence would make you trust it?** Then we practice the kind of problem the midterm asks.
:::

## Why this matters: five results that looked right {#why}

::: {.lever-box}
[Each session had a result that passed the obvious test, and the evidence that decided it]{.label}

| Session | Looked right | What decided |
|---|---|---|
| P2 · PVT | Peng–Robinson: CO₂ tank 939 kg against 938 | liquid water at 500 K: Z off by 23% with the same equation |
| P3 · residuals | ideal-gas compressor work, 3430 J/mol | reference 2865 J/mol; outlet 387.7 K against 399.7 K |
| P4 · fugacity | PR P<sup>sat</sup> of propane at 300 K, 9.975 bar against 9.977 | ω is fitted to P<sup>sat</sup>; the liquid volume is 3.8% low |
| P5 · mixtures | Lewis–Randall for 2% CO₂ in methane at 60 bar | φ̂<sub>CO₂</sub> 8% from pure CO₂; k₁₂ = 0 rules 11–37% off in B₁₂ |
| P6 · activity | NRTL fitted to G<sup>E</sup>/RT: best 80 kPa prediction | γ₁∞ = 21 against 7.7, and a liquid split that does not exist |
:::

In each case the model agreed with the data it was built on. The question was always which evidence the claim needed.

## One chain, six steps {#chain}

| Session | Working relation | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| P1 · framework | dG = −S dT + V dP; dH = C<sub>p</sub>dT + [V − T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>]dP | PVT data and C<sub>p</sub><sup>ig</sup> |
| P2 · PVT | Z = PV/RT; P = RT/(V − b) − a(T)/[(V + εb)(V + σb)]; Z = 1 + BP/RT | T<sub>c</sub>, P<sub>c</sub>, ω, or B(T) |
| P3 · residuals | H<sup>R</sup>/RT = −T∫₀<sup>P</sup>(∂Z/∂T)<sub>P</sub>dP/P; H = H<sup>ig</sup> + H<sup>R</sup> | Z(T, P) and C<sub>p</sub><sup>ig</sup> |
| P4 · pure equilibrium | ln φ = ∫₀<sup>P</sup>(Z − 1)dP/P; $f^L=\varphi^{\text{sat}}P^{\text{sat}}\mathcal{P}$ | an EOS, or P<sup>sat</sup> and V<sup>L</sup> |
| P5 · mixtures | M̄<sub>i</sub> = ∂(nM)/∂n<sub>i</sub>; Σx<sub>i</sub>dM̄<sub>i</sub> = 0; ln φ̂<sub>i</sub> = ∫₀<sup>P</sup>(Z̄<sub>i</sub> − 1)dP/P | B₁₂ or k<sub>ij</sub> |
| P6 · activity | γ<sub>i</sub> = f̂<sub>i</sub>/(x<sub>i</sub>f<sub>i</sub>°); y<sub>i</sub>Φ<sub>i</sub>P = x<sub>i</sub>γ<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> | a G<sup>E</sup> model and a standard state |

Each step uses the one before. Session 1 after the midterm joins P4–P6 into the γ–φ and φ–φ forms of VLE.

## Choosing a property model {#choosing}

::: {.lever-box}
| Situation | Start with | Check first |
|---|---|---|
| Gas or supercritical fluid, nonpolar, low density | virial, B(T) | ρ below about half of ρ<sub>c</sub> |
| Pure fluid with a reference equation of state | the reference equation (NIST) | its stated uncertainty in this region |
| Hydrocarbons and light gases, high pressure, both phases | cubic EOS (PR, SRK) with k<sub>ij</sub> | Z and P<sup>sat</sup> against data; liquid volume |
| Polar or associating liquids, low pressure | γ–φ: Wilson, NRTL, UNIQUAC; a P<sup>sat</sup> correlation | VLE in range, γ∞, stability |
| A liquid split is possible | NRTL or UNIQUAC, not Wilson | LLE data, not a VLE fit alone |
| Dilute solute, or a gas above its T<sub>c</sub> in a liquid | Henry's law, γ<sub>i</sub>* | a measured H<sub>i</sub> or γ∞ |
| No mixture data | UNIFAC or a predictive EOS | treat it as a first estimate; measure before design |
:::

[A table like this is a starting point (Carlson, 1996). The evidence for the case in hand decides.]{.howto}

## The evidence ladder {#ladder}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.lever-box}
[Weakest to strongest]{.label}

| Rung | Example before the midterm |
|---|---|
| 1 · calibration | B fitted up to 1 mol/L; NRTL fitted to G<sup>E</sup> |
| 2 · consistency | Gibbs–Duhem on measured γ; a balance that closes |
| 3 · held-out | fit at 60 kPa, predict 80 kPa: RMS y₁ 0.046 |
| 4 · independent property | PR built on P<sup>sat</sup>, checked on V<sup>L</sup>: +23% for water at 500 K |
| 5 · different method | B₁₂ measured, against a combining rule |
:::
:::
::: {.column width="46%" .rule-notes}
A claim is only as strong as the highest rung it reached.

**Extrapolation reaches none:** γ₁∞ lies beyond the most dilute point, x₁ = 0.0063.

**Some claims cannot be decided with the data in hand:** γ₁∞ of 2-propanol in water to better than tens of percent, when U(x) = 0.02 (k = 2).

[Saying so is part of the answer. Session 7 after the midterm uses the same ladder.]{.q}
:::
::::

## Where does each claim sit? {#activity-1 .activity}

[Activity 1 · 10 minutes · alone, then with a partner]{.act-label}

::: {.prompt}
Place each claim on the ladder, or mark it as an extrapolation or not resolvable with these data:
:::

1. PR gives the vapor pressure of propane at 300 K within 0.02%.
2. The virial B fitted up to 1 mol/L reproduces Z of methane at 300 K below 1 mol/L.
3. NRTL fitted at 60 kPa predicts y₁ at 80 kPa with RMS 0.047.
4. The Pitzer–Prausnitz B₁₂ for methane + ethane is within 2% of the measured value.
5. 2-propanol at infinite dilution in water has γ∞ = 7.7.
6. With a volume shift, PR describes liquid water at 500 K within 0.2%.

::: {.selfstudy}
**On your own:** pause here and write your answer. In place of a partner, compare it with the next slide and write one sentence on any difference and its cause.
:::

## Activity 1: check your answer {#activity-1-debrief}

| Claim | Where it sits | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · P<sup>sat</sup> of propane | close to calibration | ω and α(T) are built to reproduce P<sup>sat</sup>; it says nothing about V<sup>L</sup> (−3.8%) |
| 2 · Z below 1 mol/L | calibration | the same data that fixed B |
| 3 · y₁ at 80 kPa | held-out | a different pressure, not used in the fit |
| 4 · B₁₂ within 2% | held-out | pure-component data predict a mixture measurement |
| 5 · γ∞ = 7.7 | extrapolation | beyond x₁ = 0.0063; the G<sup>E</sup> fit gives 21 from the same data |
| 6 · water within 0.2% | mostly calibration | c is set from the saturated liquid at 500 K; for CO₂ at 280 K the same shift raises the error from 1.6% to 4.4% |

Four of six claims are calibration or extrapolation presented as results. Only two reached held-out data.

## Demonstration · one shift in Lab P2 {#demo-lab}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
1. Water at 500 K, Peng–Robinson. Read the dense-phase error.
2. Volume translation: **shift c so that the saturated liquid at this T is exact**. Read it again, and the vapor pressure.
3. Repeat for propane at 300 K and CO₂ at 280 K.
4. Which rung did the shift reach, and for which fluid?

[Open Lab P2 in the Graduate view →](../preview-2027/eos.html?mode=graduate){.lab-button target="_blank"}
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.lever-box}
[Peng–Robinson, mean |error| in Z above ρ<sub>c</sub> / %]{.label}

| Isotherm | c / (cm³/mol) | no shift | shifted |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| water, 500 K | +4.98 | 23.0 | 0.2 |
| propane, 300 K | −3.40 | 5.1 | 1.2 |
| CO₂, 280 K | +1.86 | 1.6 | 4.4 |
:::

::: {.expect}
[What to notice]{.label}
The shift moves every volume by c and leaves P<sup>sat</sup> unchanged (Péneloux et al., 1982). One number fitted at one state cannot correct the shape of an isotherm.
:::
:::
::::

## Problem A · a high-pressure valve {#problem-a}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.prompt}
Nitrogen at 300 K and 200 bar is throttled to 1 bar. Predict the outlet temperature with the ideal gas, the two-term virial equation, SRK and Peng–Robinson, and compare with the reference. Why does the virial equation fail here when it worked for methane from 100 to 20 bar?
:::

Sessions P1, P2 and P3.
:::
::: {.column width="48%" .rule-notes}
[Hints]{.label}

1. H<sub>out</sub> = H<sub>in</sub>; H = H<sup>ig</sup> + H<sup>R</sup> at each end.
2. Lab P3, nitrogen valve, all models.
3. Inlet density from the reference Z = 1.057. Compare it with ρ<sub>c</sub> = 11.18 mol/L.
:::
::::

## Problem B · pumping a liquid {#problem-b}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.prompt}
Liquid propane at 300 K is pumped from its vapor pressure to 50 bar. P<sup>sat</sup> = 9.977 bar, φ<sup>sat</sup> = 0.846 and V<sup>L</sup> = 90.09 cm³/mol (NIST). Compute f<sup>L</sup> at 50 bar (i) as φ<sup>sat</sup>P<sup>sat</sup>, (ii) with the Poynting factor, and (iii) with PR directly. The reference is 9.736 bar. Which assumption matters most?
:::

Session P4.
:::
::: {.column width="48%" .rule-notes}
[Hints]{.label}

1. Poynting: $\mathcal{P}=\exp[V^L(P-P^{\text{sat}})/RT]$, liquid taken as incompressible.
2. Lab P4, propane at 300 K, for (iii).
3. How much does the 3.8% error in the PR liquid volume change the Poynting factor?
:::
::::

## Problem C · a dilute solute {#problem-c}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.prompt}
Water containing 0.5 mol% 2-propanol at 345 K feeds a stripping column. P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 65.8 kPa. Estimate the partial pressure of 2-propanol above the liquid with (i) the ideal solution, (ii) the models fitted to ln γ and (iii) the models fitted to G<sup>E</sup>/RT. What value and range would you give the designer?
:::

Sessions P5 and P6.
:::
::: {.column width="48%" .rule-notes}
[Hints]{.label}

1. p₁ = x₁γ₁P₁<sup>sat</sup>; at x₁ = 0.005, γ₁ is close to γ₁∞.
2. Lab P6 A, both objectives.
3. Is the vapor ideal at this pressure? (Session P4)
:::
::::

## Activity 2 · check your answers {#activity-2-check}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.lever-box}
[A · nitrogen, 300 K, 200 → 1 bar, outlet / K]{.label}

NIST **269.2** · ideal 300.0 · virial 260.6 · SRK 271.6 · PR 265.4

The inlet is at 7.6 mol/L, 0.68 ρ<sub>c</sub>. The virial gives Z = 0.957 where the gas has 1.057: two terms cannot describe a state where repulsion dominates. Methane at 100 bar is at 0.46 ρ<sub>c</sub> (Z = 0.856; virial 0.834).
:::

::: {.lever-box}
[B · propane, 300 K, 50 bar, f<sup>L</sup> / bar]{.label}

(i) 8.44 (−13%) · (ii) **9.75** (+0.2%) · (iii) PR 9.63 (−1.1%)

Poynting factor 1.156. The PR volume changes it by 0.5%. f<sup>L</sup> ≈ P<sup>sat</sup> gives 9.98 (+2.5%) only because φ<sup>sat</sup> and Poynting nearly cancel.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.lever-box}
[C · 2-propanol, x₁ = 0.005, 345 K]{.label}

| Model | γ₁ | p₁ / kPa |
|---|---:|---:|
| ideal solution | 1 | 0.33 |
| Margules 2, ln γ | 7.32 | 2.41 |
| NRTL, ln γ | 7.45 | 2.45 |
| Wilson, ln γ | 7.54 | 2.48 |
| Margules 2, G<sup>E</sup> | 12.2 | 4.0 |
| NRTL, G<sup>E</sup> | 19.7 | 6.5 |
| Wilson, G<sup>E</sup> | 34.4 | 11.3 |

Report about 2.4–2.5 kPa from the fits that reproduce the dilute data, with an uncertainty of tens of percent, and recommend a direct γ∞ measurement.
:::

## Exam-style problem {#exam-problem}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.prompt}
A design note sizes a 1 m³ CO₂ buffer vessel at 280 K and 100 bar, and a compressor from 30 to 100 bar at 300 K inlet, with the ideal gas and "a 10% margin". (a) Quantify the error in the stored mass, the compressor work and the outlet temperature. (b) Is the margin adequate? (c) What would you use instead, and what evidence supports it?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%" .rule-notes}
[25 minutes · alone]{.label}

Answer in this order: equation, assumptions with their size, numbers, check, conclusion and its limit.

You may use the labs. State every number you take from them.
:::
::::

## Exam-style problem: a model answer {#exam-answer}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**(a)** Mass m = PVM/(ZRT). The vessel holds compressed liquid: the reference gives 938 kg, the ideal gas 189 kg (−80%). Isentropic work W = ΔH with S<sub>out</sub> = S<sub>in</sub>, H = H<sup>ig</sup> + H<sup>R</sup>: reference 2865 J/mol and 399.7 K; ideal gas 3430 J/mol (+20%) and 387.7 K (12 K low).

**(b)** No. The mass is low by a factor of 5, the unsafe direction for an inventory or release estimate. The work error is twice the margin and errs on the safe side; the outlet temperature errs on the unsafe side.
:::
::: {.column width="46%" .rule-notes}
**(c)** For pure CO₂, use the reference equation of state (Span and Wagner), from which the NIST values come. If a cubic is needed, PR gives 939 kg, 2851 J/mol and 403.4 K. That agreement is a held-out check (rung 3) at two states: PR uses only T<sub>c</sub>, P<sub>c</sub> and ω. Near the critical point (T<sub>r</sub> = 1.05) its dense-phase Z error rises to 5.3%, so check it again if the conditions move.

[A margin covers known, bounded uncertainty. It does not cover using a model outside the region where it holds.]{.q}
:::
::::

## How answers are marked {#marking}

::: {.mistakes}
::: {}
**Equation and reference state (25 %).** The right relation, with the reference state, units and path stated.
:::
::: {}
**Assumptions with their size (20 %).** Not "assume an ideal vapor", but "φ̂ = 1 changes p₁ by about 1%".
:::
::: {}
**Numbers that can be checked (25 %).** Intermediate values, units, and a balance or limit that closes.
:::
::: {}
**Conclusion and its limit (30 %).** What the evidence supports, which rung it reached, what would raise it.
:::
:::

A correct number with no limit stated earns less than a well-argued answer with an arithmetic slip.

## Summary {#summary}

::: {.summary3}
::: {}
[One chain]{.label}
PVT and C<sub>p</sub><sup>ig</sup> give Z, residual properties, fugacity; mixtures add composition, liquids add γ.
:::
::: {}
[Choosing]{.label}
Start from the fluid, the phase and the pressure. Then check the property the result depends on, in the region of use.
:::
::: {}
[Evidence]{.label}
Calibration, consistency, held-out, independent property, different method. A claim is only as strong as its highest rung.
:::
:::

**Session question:** choose by fluid, phase and pressure, then test the model on a property it was not built on. The strongest evidence before the midterm was of that kind: the liquid volume against a P<sup>sat</sup>-fitted EOS, 80 kPa VLE against a 60 kPa fit, a measured B₁₂ against a combining rule.
